props.title: The Power of the Dog
props.initialSlug: Toxic masculinity unravels on a 1920s Montana ranch

sections.content: Jane Campion's **The Power of the Dog (2021)** (2021) masterfully reinvents the Western through a psychological lens, much like what There Will Be Blood (2007) accomplished with its oil-baron narrative. The film's exploration of repressed sexuality and toxic masculinity through Benedict Cumberbatch's Phil Burbank echoes the complex character work in Brokeback Mountain (2005), but with a more sinister, calculated approach. Campion's direction creates a suffocating atmosphere reminiscent of The Piano (1993), where the New Zealand landscape similarly became a character itself.

sections.content: The film's exploration of masculine power dynamics recalls classic revisionist Westerns like **McCabe & Mrs. Miller** (1971) and **Unforgiven** (1992), but through a distinctly modern lens. Cinematographer Ari Wegner's work transforms Montana's landscape into a psychological battleground, much like how Days of Heaven (1978) used natural light to elevate its narrative beyond mere period drama. The tension between Phil and Peter creates a psychological thriller framework that owes more to **In Cold Blood** (1967) than traditional Westerns.

Campion's attention to period detail and emotional authenticity builds on themes she explored in The Piano (1993), while adding layers of menace and sexual tension that recall Portrait of a Lady on Fire (2019). The film's examination of queerness in the American West creates a dialogue with both historical revisionism and contemporary gender studies, similar to how **The Assassination of Jesse James by the Coward Robert Ford** (2007) deconstructed Western mythology. SUBHEAD: Deconstructing the Modern Western

sections.content: **The Power of the Dog** (2021) joins films like **No Country for Old Men** (2007) and **Wind River** (2017) in reimagining Western themes for contemporary audiences. The film's psychological complexity and attention to repressed emotion creates a bridge between classic character studies like **Giant** (1956) and modern examinations of masculinity like **Manchester by the Sea** (2016). Jonny Greenwood's score enhances the psychological tension, creating an atmosphere that owes as much to There Will Be Blood (2007) as it does to traditional Western soundtracks.
